sections.h2: What and where is Cascade County, Montana?
sections.html:
Cascade County is a north-central Montana county whose seat is Great Falls, and it takes its name from the falls on the Missouri River. According to its Wikipedia entry, it was created in 1887, covers 2,711 square miles (2,698 of them land) and had 84,414 residents in the 2020 census, the fifth-highest total among Montana counties.

Teton County lies to the northwest, Chouteau to the northeast, Judith Basin to the east, Meagher to the south and Lewis and Clark to the west. Great Falls is the only city. The towns are Belt, Cascade and Neihart, and census-designated places include Black Eagle, Centerville, Fort Shaw, Sand Coulee, Simms, Sun River, Ulm and Vaughn. Malmstrom Air Force Base is listed as its own place as well.

Public land takes in Benton Lake National Wildlife Refuge and part of the Lewis and Clark National Forest. For a seller, the spread from a city lot in Great Falls to a house in Sand Coulee or Simms is wide, and each location answers different buyer questions about wells, septic systems and winter road access.

sections.h2: How much does Malmstrom Air Force Base matter to the local housing picture?
sections.html:
Malmstrom Air Force Base is the biggest employer name in Cascade County, and the base reports about $444 million in annual economic impact for fiscal year 2025. The figure comes from the base's own commander's data card, which breaks it into $285.8 million in payroll, $45.5 million in expenditures and an estimate for jobs the base supports indirectly.

The same card lists 3,896 assigned Department of the Air Force personnel, 3,371 of them military and 525 civilian, along with 2,817 dependents. It also says 609 military dependents attend Great Falls schools, and that the base has 1,116 privatized housing units. The 341st Missile Wing operates 150 launch facilities across a missile complex of 13,800 square miles, which is why so many rural Cascade County parcels sit near government sites.

Wikipedia adds that in 2009 Benefis, Great Falls Clinic, National Electronics Warranty and Walmart were among the largest private employers. That list is old, so treat it as background. What it suggests for a house sale is simple: a good share of local demand follows base assignments and hospital employment, and sellers who are relocating on a short timeline often need a quick close.

sections.h2: What does the 2026 Montana tax structure mean for a Cascade County house?
sections.html:
For tax year 2026, a primary residence or long-term rental is taxed at 0.76 percent on the first $378,000 of market value, 0.90 percent from $378,001 to $756,000, 1.10 percent up to $1,511,999 and 1.90 percent above that. The Montana Department of Revenue publishes the schedule on its 2026 tax information page. Second homes, short-term rentals and vacant residential lots pay a flat 1.90 percent.

Those percentages produce a taxable value, and the county then applies the combined mills of every local district to reach a bill. As an illustration of the first step only, the Census median owner-occupied value shown earlier on this page, $243,300, falls entirely in the first bracket and yields a taxable value of about $1,849. Your actual bill depends on the mills for your city, school district and special districts.

The reduced rate is called the homestead rate. Eligible homes include single-family houses, townhomes, condos and manufactured homes with up to one acre of land, when the owner lives there at least seven months of the year.

sections.h2: Does the reduced rate transfer when a Cascade County house is sold?
sections.html:
No. The Department of Revenue says an approved homestead rate stays on the property through the end of the calendar year even if ownership changes, but the new owner must apply to keep it in the following year. For the 2027 tax year the enrollment period closes on March 1, 2027, according to the department's homestead FAQ.

That detail matters for investors who buy a house to rent. A long-term rental can qualify when it is rented for 28 or more days for at least seven months of the year, but the owner has to apply during the window. An investor who skips the application, or rents the house on a short-term basis, faces the flat 1.90 percent rate.

  • Seller: keep your last tax bill and the homestead approval for the title company.
  • Buyer who will live in the house: enroll as the new owner before March 1.
  • Buyer who will rent long term: apply in the rental window and plan on seven months of qualifying use.

sections.h2: When are Cascade County property taxes due, and can they be paid in installments?
sections.html:
Half of the tax is due by 5 p.m. on November 30, or within 30 days after the tax notice is postmarked if that is later, and the other half is due by 5 p.m. on May 31. The rule is in Montana Code 15-16-102. If a due date lands on a holiday or Saturday, payment is timely through 5 p.m. on the next business day.

A taxpayer enrolled in the alternative payment schedule for primary residences pays one-seventh of the total on the last day of each month from November 30 through May 31. The seven payments fall on November 30, December 31, January 31, February 28, March 31, April 30 and May 31. The Cascade County Treasurer's property tax page says it offers two payment plan options, including this 7-payment plan for real estate.

A late payment is delinquent and draws interest at 5/6 of 1 percent a month, plus a 2 percent penalty on the delinquent amount. The law also lets you pay the current year without catching up older delinquent taxes, but any payment toward delinquency goes to the oldest year first, and paying the current year does not release the lien on an earlier year.

sections.h2: How do you challenge a Cascade County valuation?
sections.html:
Valuation disputes start with the Montana Department of Revenue, not the county treasurer. The department states that you may request an informal review on Form AB-26 within 30 days of the date on your classification and appraisal notice, or appeal directly to the county tax appeal board by filing with the county clerk and recorder within the same 30 days.

The 2025 to 2026 valuation cycle uses a January 1, 2024 valuation date. Evidence the department accepts includes your own market estimate as of that date, a purchase price within six months of it, a fee appraisal, comparable sales and listings from the same window, and a builder's cost breakdown for remodels. Before filing, you can check your square footage and room counts on Property.MT.gov and call your DOR field office to talk with an appraiser.

If you disagree with the informal decision, you can appeal to the county tax appeal board, an independent board appointed by county commissioners. The Montana Tax Appeal Board is the next step, and district court follows. To protect a refund, Montana law requires a written protest filed with the county treasurer along with payment of the disputed tax by the due date. Cascade County's protest form notes it must be filed before the first Monday in June or within 30 days of a notice of classification and appraisal or of a review determination.

sections.h2: What if a Cascade County seller is behind on taxes or owns a mobile home?
sections.html:
The county treasurer collects delinquent real property taxes through a lien on the real estate, and for mobile homes the treasurer can seek a writ of execution. A county letter on the topic says mobile home owners with delinquent taxes get a chance to pay in full or set up a payment program before further steps.

For a house, the practical path is to get a payoff figure and settle it from sale proceeds. The title company will pull the tax record, and any delinquent amount, penalty and interest is deducted at closing. Selling to a buyer who purchases for cash can simplify that step because there is no loan approval waiting on the payoff.

Before you list or accept an offer, it helps to collect these items:

  • Your latest tax statement and any protest or AB-26 paperwork.
  • Proof of homestead enrollment, if you have it.
  • The Malmstrom or employer orders that set your move date, if a transfer drives the sale.

faqs.q: Who handles property tax bills in Cascade County, Montana?
faqs.a: The Cascade County Treasurer's Office collects and bills the tax. The Montana Department of Revenue sets valuation and handles assessment appeals, so questions about the appraised value go to the department.

faqs.q: Can I pay Cascade County property tax in seven payments?
faqs.a: Yes, if you are enrolled in the alternative payment schedule for a primary residence. One-seventh is due on the last day of each month from November 30 through May 31, under Montana Code 15-16-122. The county application form must be filed to enroll.

faqs.q: What is the penalty for late property tax in Montana?
faqs.a: Delinquent tax draws interest at 5/6 of 1 percent per month and a 2 percent penalty. Taxes are delinquent after 5 p.m. on November 30 for the first half and after 5 p.m. on May 31 for the second half.

faqs.q: Does a buyer keep my homestead tax rate?
faqs.a: Not automatically. The rate stays on the property through the end of the calendar year of the sale, and the new owner must submit a homestead application to keep it for the next year.

faqs.q: Can I sell my Cascade County house for cash if taxes are owed?
faqs.a: Yes. Unpaid taxes, penalty and interest come out of the proceeds at closing, and the title company confirms the amount with the county treasurer.
